progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b06: innate defences hold a pathogen back while the adaptive response builds; adaptive responses take days the first time. From b07: antigens; each B cell has one receptor shape; clonal selection and expansion; plasma cells release antibodies; memory B cells "stay for later" (named only); antibodies block, clump and coat pathogens. From b08: T cells, antigen presentation, helper and cytotoxic T cells; some T cells become memory T cells (named only). From Year 11 and b01: viruses are not cells. Not assumed: primary and secondary response, memory cells in action, the antibody graph, vaccination, vaccine types, boosters, active and passive immunity, natural and artificial immunity, antivenom.
progression.startsWith: Compare primary and secondary responses. The video opens: Most people who've had chickenpox don't catch it again.
progression.stopsAfter: describing the primary response (only a few fitting B and T cells; selection and division take days; antibody appears after a week or more; illness while it builds); explaining what remains (antibody falls far below its peak as most plasma cells die; long-lived memory B and T cells, far more fitting cells than before, so memory is stored mainly in cells); explaining the secondary response (many fitting cells already waiting, so the antigen meets them quickly, fewer divisions, memory B cells quickly become plasma cells, memory helper T cells give the go-ahead quickly and memory cytotoxic T cells destroy infected cells sooner; antibody rises within days, much higher, lasts longer; often cleared before illness); reading a primary and secondary antibody graph, including that memory applies only to the same antigen; explaining vaccination as a safe first exposure (weakened live, killed, a protein, or instructions to make a protein) giving memory without the illness, and boosters as a later extra dose; naming both active and passive immunity as acquired immunity, unlike innate defences; distinguishing active immunity (own response, memory, often long-lasting, slow to build; natural by infection, artificial by vaccine) from passive immunity (antibodies made by another person or animal, immediate, receiving them makes no memory cells, fades over weeks to months; natural from the mother across the placenta and in breast milk, artificial by injection such as antivenom); choosing between them in a situation.
progression.nextLesson: immune response practice (route entry bio-m7-g03), then how hygiene and quarantine interrupt spread (bio-m7-b10).

teaching.task: Most people who've had chickenpox don't catch it again. What changed after the first infection, and how do vaccines and antibody injections give protection?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why the first response is slow (few fitting cells must be selected and multiply; scene 2); why antibody falls but protection stays (plasma cells die, memory cells remain; scene 3, answering the hook's surprise); why the second response is faster and bigger (more fitting cells waiting, fewer divisions, fast change to plasma cells; scene 4); why memory doesn't help against a new antigen (scene 5); how a vaccine gives memory without illness (scene 7); why a booster helps (scene 8); why passive immunity is immediate but temporary (ready-made antibodies, no selection, broken down; scene 10); when passive immunity is the only choice (scene 11). Visible case: the same graph and the same cell field change in place from first infection to second exposure. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; scenes 4 (cells and graph together) and 7 (vaccine types) are the densest, so each earlier tag or label dims.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Most people who have had chickenpox do not catch it again, so the question is what changed after the first infection and how vaccines and antibody injections give protection. In the first infection only a few B and T cells fit the virus, so they must be selected and multiply, and antibodies take days to rise; when the infection is cleared most plasma cells die and the antibody level falls, but memory B and T cells stay. On a second exposure many fitting cells are already waiting, so the response starts sooner, makes much more antibody and lasts longer, and the antibody graph shows a slow, low primary hump against a fast, tall secondary peak, often on a log scale. Vaccination gives the antigen in a form that does not cause the full disease, so the first response happens safely and memory cells form, and a booster triggers a secondary response. Vaccines and infections give active immunity because your own system made the memory cells, while passive immunity gives ready-made antibodies that work at once but fade and leave no memory, with antivenom as artificial passive immunity. Both are acquired immunity, and two questions sort any case: are there memory cells for this antigen, and who made the antibodies. The memory aid is second exposure, faster, bigger, longer. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Most people who've had chickenpox don't catch it again. Years later, they can breathe in the same virus and usually don't get sick. You might think that's because antibodies from the first time are still in their blood. But by then, the antibody level has usually fallen far below its peak. So what's stopping the virus?
teaching.understandingCheck: 13a explains a two-antigen antibody graph (primary against secondary response, the route's start, and specificity of memory). 13c evaluates a claim that antivenom has made a bushwalker immune (passive against active immunity, the route's stop). Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it. Feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): the answer, the key reasons, givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B7-IQ3-02 (p 54): "explain how the immune system responds after primary exposure to a pathogen, including innate and acquired immunity". B7-IQ4-02 (p 55): "investigate procedures that can be employed to prevent the spread of disease, including but not limited to: (ACSBL124)", with the listed item "vaccination, including passive and active immunity (ACSBL100, ACSBL123)". Verb "explain" (B7-IQ3-02): scenes 3 to 5 give the cause of each difference between the responses (more fitting cells waiting, fewer divisions, fast change to plasma cells). "Acquired immunity" in the dotpoint is taught as active immunity acquired naturally or artificially (scene 9), with innate immunity recalled as the response that holds the pathogen back during the primary lag (scene 2, one clause). "Investigate" (B7-IQ4-02): attempt 1 interprets a two-antigen experiment; attempt 2 applies the active and passive distinction to a real procedure.

design.visualSystem: One memory board. Left two-thirds: a coded antibody graph (b07's style; the house coded `lineGraph`, never an AI image) on which the response is drawn as each step is narrated: x axis "time after first exposure (days)", y axis "antibody level" (log scale in scenes 5 and 13a, tagged), exposure markers as small amber arrows on the x axis. Beside or above the graph, painted cells show what the curve is caused by: a cell count field of small `m7-b-cell-bare-v1.png` copies (with a few `m7-t-cell-v1.png` copies) in which the cells that fit the virus are lit teal: two or three before the first infection, many after it. Plasma cells (`m7-plasma-cell-v1.png`) appear when antibody rises and fade when it falls. The virus is a new `m7-varicella-virus-v1.png`. Scenes 7 and 8 add the existing `m7-vaccine-vial-syringe-v1.png`. Scenes 9 to 12 build the coded two-by-two table (rows "active", "passive"; columns "natural", "artificial"), one quadrant per cue, each with one painted thumbnail: the varicella virus (natural active), the vaccine vial (artificial active), the new `m7-placenta-villus-v1.png` with the existing `b3a2-milk-gland-full-v1.png` (natural passive) and the new `m7-brown-snake-v1.png` (artificial passive). Right third, small: b06 to b08's `ResponseStrip`, complete, with memory cells marked at the foot of both adaptive columns (scene 3). No people, hands or faces: no child with chickenpox, no arm being injected, no mother or baby (the existing `b3a-fetus-placenta-v1.png` shows a fetus and is not used); the body appears only as cells, a placental villus and a gland. The snake is an animal, painted alone with no person. Coded elements are abstract only: the graph, the cell count field layout, the table, arrows, chips, glosses and the strip. Scale: B cell about 8 µm, plasma cell about 12 µm (scaled up uniformly against the B cell plate as in b07, never stretched), T cell about 7 µm; the varicella virus (about 0.2 µm) is only ever shown as its own enlarged plate with a grey tag "drawn far larger than real"; the placental villus close-up spans about 0.2 mm. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides small grey labels; earlier chips dim to grey. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched.
